negative-current-density.title: Negative Current Density
negative-current-density.conceptual_definition: A vector field representing the spatial density and direction of flow of negative charge, or a specific component/type of current in a physical system.
negative-current-density.intuitive_summary: It quantifies the rate at which negative charge passes through a unit area perpendicular to the flow, or describes a particular aspect of current flow at a given point in space.
negative-current-density.interpretation: The symbol $J$ typically denotes current density, a vector quantity whose direction is the direction of charge flow and whose magnitude is the amount of charge per unit time per unit area. The superscript `'-'` can signify several physical contexts. Most commonly, it refers to the current density specifically due to the motion of negative charges (e.g., electrons in a conductor). In more advanced theoretical physics, particularly in quantum field theory, it could represent a specific component of a current, such as a left-handed (chiral) current in the context of weak interactions, or a current associated with antiparticles. Its precise meaning is highly dependent on the specific physical theory and context in which it is used.
negative-current-density.symmetry_origin: If $J^-(x)$ represents a conserved current (e.g., electric charge current), its conservation is a direct consequence of a continuous global or local gauge symmetry via Noether's theorem. For instance, the conservation of electric charge current is linked to the $U(1)$ gauge symmetry of electromagnetism. If it's a chiral current, its properties are tied to specific symmetries of the underlying field theory, such as chiral symmetry.
negative-current-density.limits_and_boundary: As a current density, $J^-(x)$ must satisfy the continuity equation, $\partial_\mu J^\mu = 0$ (in relativistic notation) or $\nabla \cdot J + \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0$ (in non-relativistic notation), where $\rho$ is the corresponding charge density. This equation expresses the local conservation of the charge or quantity associated with the current. At boundaries between different media, specific boundary conditions apply, often related to the conservation of current components perpendicular to the surface.

J^-.description: A vector field representing the flow of negative charge or a specific component/type of current.

x.name: Position Vector
x.description: The spatial coordinate at which the current density is evaluated.

electromagnetic-field-tensor.title: Electromagnetic Field Tensor
electromagnetic-field-tensor.conceptual_definition: The electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu\nu}$ is an antisymmetric second-rank tensor that unifies the electric and magnetic fields into a single relativistic entity, derived from the four-potential $A_\mu$.
electromagnetic-field-tensor.intuitive_summary: This tensor provides a compact and covariant description of the electromagnetic field, simplifying Maxwell's equations and demonstrating the relativistic interdependence of electric and magnetic phenomena.
electromagnetic-field-tensor.interpretation: The electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu\nu}$ is a crucial object in relativistic electromagnetism, combining the components of the electric field $\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$ into a single $4 \times 4$ antisymmetric matrix. Its components are defined such that $F_{0i} = -F_{i0} = E_i/c$ and $F_{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk} B_k$, where $c$ is the speed of light and $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol. This formulation inherently satisfies two of Maxwell's equations (Faraday's law and Gauss's law for magnetism) as identities, provided the four-potential $A_\mu$ is well-defined. The tensor transforms covariantly under Lorentz transformations, meaning its form is preserved in all inertial frames, thereby explicitly demonstrating the relativistic nature of electromagnetism.

F_{\\mu\\nu}.name: Electromagnetic Field Tensor
F_{\\mu\\nu}.description: The antisymmetric second-rank electromagnetic field tensor, whose components represent the electric and magnetic fields in a relativistic framework. Specifically, $F_{0i} = E_i/c$ and $F_{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk} B_k$.

\\partial_\\mu.name: Four-gradient
\\partial_\\mu.description: The four-gradient operator, defined as $(\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}, \vec{\nabla})$, where $c$ is the speed of light, $t$ is time, and $\vec{\nabla}$ is the spatial gradient operator.

A_\\nu.name: Four-potential
A_\\nu.description: The electromagnetic four-potential, a four-vector defined as $(\frac{\Phi}{c}, \vec{A})$, where $\Phi$ is the scalar potential and $\vec{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential.
